body.text: The Interview: Spooky Ladies takes bewitching look at lives of lady magicians, mediums and frauds

Were the great magicians and mediums of the 20th century actually women? That's the big question in author Kaz Cooke's surprising and seriously charming new book, Spooky Ladies, out just in time for Halloween.

The stalwart of Australian publishing became a household name for books like Up the Duff: The Real Guide to Pregnancy, Girl Stuff, Babies and Toddlers and It's the Menopause. But Cooke has recently published works such as You're Doing It Wrong, which looks at historically terrible advice for women about health and behaviour.

Her new one takes on the long history of magic and mediumship, especially the spiritualism movement of the late 19th century, through the lens of under-reported lives of the women — all with trademark wit.

From Lady Conan Doyle, wife of the famous Arthur, to the thriving mediumship scene of 1800s Melbourne, Cooke gives texture and context to the stories of women who used magic and vibes to make themselves rich and famous.
You're best known for helping women with books about pregnancy, birth and child-rearing. What inspired you to write about spooky ladies?

Well, over the last few years, I have found that an archive is my happy place. And I have loved looking at women who are no longer with us, who might have been forgotten or erased by history in some way, or misunderstood.

I became fascinated by the idea that there was a gender divide often between magicians and mediums. And then I realised, oh no, there were heaps of women magicians. They just didn't get written about.
And a lot of the famous wives, like Mrs Houdini, Bess, were just always kind of presumed to be timid or to be decorative by the male biographers of the magicians.
It's fascinating to me too that a lot of these women, they were opportunistic and they were frauds and they were incredibly talented at the acts they did.

The story of Lady Conan Doyle is one of the most interesting in the book and it seems you did not love her. She and Arthur Conan Doyle (author of Sherlock Holmes) and their social milieu intersected so much with 20th-century history. What did you learn there?
I really loved Sherlock Holmes as a big kid. So, I had not realised, like a lot of people, what an extraordinarily dim man he was and how he was a con man who didn't know he was a con man.
The way that his second wife Lady Conan Doyle has been written about before is that she was this marvellous English rose, you know, with fine upstanding morals.
But she was just a dreadful woman manipulating her husband by pretending to be a medium and doing the easiest version of mediuming that she could, which was automatic writing.
Why was spiritualism so appealing to the elites of the time?

Spiritualism was appealing to lots of people. I think all these women I've written about are emblematic of their times. Spiritualism started out as a girlish prank and then became a religion, and I think that's got a lot to do with people wanting to believe that we can communicate with people who have died.

Also, it was the age of scientific discovery. So, they were discovering things that you couldn't see, like magnetism and electricity. People kind of wanted to believe that maybe there was this whole spirit world that we couldn't see. A lot of people were just trying to make money and were just frauds.
But a lot of it had to do with the idea of women being ethereal and not very clever, so the spirits would kind of use them just as a conduit. Women were simply tubes!
Tubes! That's a theme in your work I suppose. That's what pregnancy is. You just get treated like a very large test tube.
Yes, absolutely.
One other thing about younger women dashing about in the drawing room after dark is that it's fun. I think it was entertainment. People didn't have streaming services. They used it to survive.

And what I realised was just how much, along with all the glamour, there was just so much grit and determination. They had no pensions, no health care, very often carrying the act if they were a magician, but just being dismissed as, you know, a bit of fluff on the side.
Tell me about the research you did for this book.

I got to go to Texas in between the two Trump presidencies, to the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas in Austin for a couple of weeks. They have a collection there of his magic files on other magicians.
So aside from obeying the sign that said I wasn't allowed to leave my handgun in the locker, I was in absolute heaven.

For example, I found the original love notes that Harry Houdini would leave on the pillow for Bess. Biographers and novelists have always said that Houdini's relationship with Bess was really childlike and he was sickly sweet and sentimental. But when you see and read the real thing, you can absolutely see that they were both in on the joke.

I got quite cross about the way that Bess Houdini had been written about as if she was this timid person who was always worried and didn't understand how the act worked. It's almost libellous. You can't libel the dead, as you well know, but I was sort of indignant on her behalf.
I think these women have been viewed in lots of ways, but all of the ways are one-dimensional.
Some of the research was also in Australia. Tell me about that.

There was a lot. I was so excited when I realised that Moi-Yo Miller, who was a girl from Geelong who escaped the Nazis, had living relatives. She was incredibly glamorous and clever and a recognised magician's assistant.

Her daughter, Charisse, and granddaughter, Celeste, live in Melbourne and they came over and chatted for hours. Then they so kindly left Moi-Yo's own scrapbooks with me for a couple of weeks so I could go through them.

After that I said to them: "Look, there's this guy in this other book that says this really sexist thing. I don't think that's right." They corrected a lot of stuff that was on the record, and that was incredibly useful.
Whereas for a lot of the others in the book, sometimes you'd have to read six books about a male magician to get a few paragraphs about his wife, who was an equal partner.
My final question for you is if you had to run a spooky grift, what would it be?

That's a great question! I've actually thought about finding some performers who'd be interested in doing the mind-reading act that Agnes Zancig did, but the problem with that is that we just haven't got the time. You have to memorise so many codes.
I think if I was to do a grift, I think it would have to involve dress-ups. I'd like to dress like Adelaide Herrmann. I could do with a tiara and a bit of diaphanous carry-on, I reckon.
Spooky Ladies is published by Scribner.
